analysis.evidence: יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים is the subject, אֶת־הָאָדָם marks the human as the direct object, and עָפָר מִן־הָאֲדָמָה identifies the material as dust from the ground.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־ and no suffix.

analysis.evidence: In יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים, “Yahweh God,” אֱלֹהִים stands in apposition to the name. The phrase identifies the subject of וַיִּיצֶר, “formed,” as Yahweh.
analysis.morphology: Proper noun without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Personal name of the God of Israel

analysis.evidence: In יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים, אֱלֹהִים stands in apposition to the name יַהְוֶה. The singular verbs וַיִּיצֶר (“he formed”) and וַיִּפַּח (“he breathed”) describe the actions of this one subject.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine plural absolute, with a singular referent.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּיצֶר יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים אֶת הָאָדָם, יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים is the subject of וַיִּיצֶר ‘formed’, and אֶת marks הָאָדָם ‘the man’ as the one formed.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle, unsuffixed, in the form אֶת.

analysis.evidence: אֶת marks הָאָדָם as the definite object of וַיִּיצֶר, “he formed.” The verse follows this individual from his formation out of dust to the moment God breathes into his nostrils.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ prefixed to a masculine singular common noun in the absolute state.

analysis.evidence: עָפָר names the material from which God formed the human. The following phrase מִן הָאֲדָמָה identifies its source, yielding “dust from the ground.”
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine singular absolute, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In עָפָר מִן הָאֲדָמָה, “dust from the ground,” מִן marks הָאֲדָמָה as the source of the dust from which God formed the human.
analysis.morphology: Independent preposition without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: out of, made from; from (a source or giver)

analysis.evidence: In עָפָר מִן הָאֲדָמָה, “dust from the ground,” מִן marks the ground as the source of the dust from which God forms the man.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, feminine singular absolute, with the prefixed definite article הָ־.
analysis.sense: earth, as the stuff things are made of

draft.change: Add the Hebrew verb נָפַח under נפח with its Qal sense of breathing into someone or something.
draft.definition: To breathe out into someone or something.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 2:7 Yahweh God breathes the breath of life into the nostrils of the man he has formed.

analysis.evidence: Yahweh God continues as the subject of וַיִּפַּח. The object נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים identifies what he breathed, the breath of life, and בְּאַפָּיו gives its destination, into the man's nostrils. The next clause gives the result: the man became a living being.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ and no suffix. The initial root consonant נ assimilates to פ, marked by the dagesh in פּ.
analysis.sense: To breathe out into someone or something.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּפַּח בְּאַפָּיו נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים, God breathes the breath of life into the man's nostrils. The suffix refers to הָאָדָם, and בְּ marks where the breath enters.
analysis.morphology: Preposition בְּ + masculine dual construct noun + third-person masculine singular possessive suffix.
analysis.sense: nostrils as the seat of breath and life

analysis.evidence: נִשְׁמַת is in construct with חַיִּים, forming “breath of life.” The phrase names what God blew into the man’s nostrils, after which the man became a living being.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, feminine singular construct, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים, “breath of life,” חַיִּים completes the construct phrase begun by נִשְׁמַת. God breathes this breath into the man's nostrils, and the man becomes a living being.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute noun, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: life as given by God's breath

analysis.evidence: הָאָדָם is the subject, and לְנֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה expresses the resulting state. When God breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, the man became a living being.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: הָאָדָם is the subject of וַיְהִי and refers back to the man God formed earlier in the verse. After God breathed into his nostrils, the man became a living being.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the absolute state with the prefixed definite article הָ־.

analysis.evidence: After God breathes the breath of life into the man's nostrils, וַיְהִי הָאָדָם לְנֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה says that the man became a living being. נֶפֶשׁ denotes the being, and חַיָּה supplies “living.”
analysis.morphology: Common noun, singular absolute, with prefixed לְ marking the result. The adjective חַיָּה shows feminine agreement.

analysis.evidence: In לְנֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, חַיָּה agrees with the feminine singular noun נֶפֶשׁ. After God breathes into his nostrils, the man becomes “a living being.”
